titleStmt.title: On Probabilistic Timing Analysis of Fault-Tolerant Real-Time Systems Experiencing Random Errors

analytic.title: On Probabilistic Timing Analysis of Fault-Tolerant Real-Time Systems Experiencing Random Errors

div.p: The inherent intractability of probabilistic timing and schedulability analysis of real-time and embedded systems in exact cases has been well discussed in the literature. This has prompted the search for efficient solutions which give meaningful results in practical situations. As many real-time systems are exposed to errors which are random in nature (e.g., due to EMI), it is prudent to consider stochastic schedulability analysis in which the impacts of such errors upon timing are considered. However, work in this area has progressed slowly: in this paper, progress is presented as follows. New schedulability conditions are derived for Earliest Deadline First (EDF)-scheduled periodic and/or sporadic task sets experiencing Binomially distributed random error arrivals, leading to job faults and re-execution attempts. A new analytic model for tightly bounding the impacts of errors over a section of the EDF workload is first presented, and subsequently used to derive an accurate and tractable probabilistic schedulability and timing analysis procedure. The analysis is sufficient to verify that task deadlines are met with a pre-specified upper tail probability R >> 0.5. An example illustrates its application and efficiency. The paper is concluded by highlighting areas of future work.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: mbedded and real-time control systems consist of single or multiple processing units which are encapsulated by the devices under their control and directly interfaced to external signals [1] [2]. By their nature, they will often have stringent timing constraints in addition to their functional specification. These constraints are related to application-level safety considerations, for example in automotive and avionic control-by-x applications. In such cases it is prudent (and often a legal requirement) to formally verify the timing properties of such systems [3] [4]. The inherent intractability of probabilistic timing and schedulability analysis of real-time and embedded systems in exact cases has been well discussed in the literature, and this has prompted the search for efficient solutions applicable to real-world cases. This paper is concerned with development of a new, tractable probabilistic timing analysis for optimal real-time embedded systems which experience random errors during operation through exposure to environmental phenomenon such as Electro Magnetic Interference (EMI) and Alpha Particle strikes.

div.head: A. Scope
div.p: The focus of the paper is upon real-time task systems scheduled using the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) dynamic scheduling technique, which is optimal for uniprocessor task scheduling and broadcast network scheduling in preemptive and (non-idling) limited/non-preemptive environments [1][5] [6]. Application services are assumed implemented in the form of a fixed number of recurring periodic/sporadic tasks with periods/deadlines derived from higher-level performance constraints [7]. Although the focus of the paper is upon probabilistic scheduling and timing analysis, it is assumed that appropriate techniques have been applied to design, implement, and verify the functional and safety-related aspects of the system, and adequate means are in place to detect run-time anomalies and invoke error handlers (see, e.g. [4] and references therein).

div.head: B. State-of-the-Art
div.p: Early approaches to incorporate random errors in schedulability analysis of real-time systems has typically assumed quasi-deterministic behavior of error arrival patterns, most notably their treatment as periodic and/or sporadic events (see, e.g. [8] [10][11][12][13][14]). Work in the area was significantly motivated by the need for practical methods to verify timing properties of the Controller Area Network (CAN), widely deployed in automotive control applications from the 1980s to present day [8]. A CAN network supports Fixed-Priority (FP) non-preemptive scheduling of messages in a shared broadcast environment. CAN networks can oftentimes operate in harsh conditions, with Bit Error Rate (BER) experimentally measured to be high as 10 -5 in 'aggressive' environments [9], with 10 -3 reported in some extreme case such as within proximity to power transmission lines [10]. Broster & Burns in [8] present early work related to timing analysis of transiently faulted CAN networks, with error arrivals assumed as sporadic (quasiperiodic) events with minimum temporal separation. The authors propose upper bounding techniques to limit the latest time that a CAN message instance in a particular stream can be scheduled for (re-)transmission following one or more faults due to EMI disturbance. The bound is used to set run-time checks which override the native CAN persistent retransmission scheme, such that harmful system-wide cascading deadline misses can be avoided. The per-message bounds are calculated using an estimate of worst-case response times in the presence of worst-case error arrivals, which are assumed quasi-periodic (sporadic) with a minimal temporal separation. A survey paper by Gardner & Liu summarises research related to overload detection and recovery for EDF [11]. The techniques typically rely upon the detection of a task exceeding its execution budget and the application of corrective actions, such as with the Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) [12]. Although the importance of these works cannot be neglected, there is no direct link to any underlying error model which ultimately leads to the overload. Lima & Burns [13] present a schedulability analysis for fixed priority (c.f. dynamic priority/deadline) scheduled systems which a certain number fixed N of faults can be present. Extension of the analysis to EDF is relatively straightforward. Although presenting an interesting contribution, no error or fault arrival pattern is assumed in the work, and no link is made to an underlying statistical error model or error arrival pattern. Short (2016) presents a schedulability and timing analysis for fully nonpreemptive EDF tasks [14], and although thorough treatment is given, the assumption is again made of periodic/sporadic error arrivals with guaranteed minimum separation between errors.

Motivated by the need to link statistical error models within the framework of timing analysis, the use of probabilistic concentration inequalities within the framework of schedulability analysis was proposed by Short & Proenza [15]. Concentration inequalities (typically of the Chernoff/Hoeffding exponential form, see e.g. [16]) provide safe bounds on upper and lower tail measures of concentration over the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of many sub-Gaussian distributions, including Poisson and Binomial models. The work in [15] employed a loose Chernoff-type expression to introduce a safe, analytical expression into schedulability analysis. The issue of the intractability inherent in probabilistic timing and schedulability analysis of real-time systems in exact cases is discussed further in [17], which also highlights the importance of the emergence of analytical approximations such as that first appearing in [15] to support computation of deadline-miss probability.

As discussed in [15] and [17], for timing and schedulability analysis for EDF and other forms of priority scheduling, there is often a need to work not directly with the CDF of an error model but rather its inverse (Quantile function). Subsequently, several error models and related concentration inequalities employed in the context of real-time systems have been developed; a relatively recent summary is presented by [17]. Motivated by the need for accurate and simple CDF and Quantile function inequalities for common distributions encountered in many Engineering and Informatics applications, related work by the author has considered both Poisson [16] and Binomial [18] cases specifically. In particular, the new range of analytically simple yet provably sharp and asymptotically exact relations proven in [18] provide a means to develop and extend previous work related to EDF scheduling in the presence of random errors.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: In this paper, a specific mathematical modelling and analysis framework is presented to model the arrival process of random errors in an EDF scheduled real-time system assuming Binomial arrival patterns. A sharp Quantile inequality is employed to produce an analytic error function which can provide a formal guarantee (for pre-specified upper tail confidence probability R) on error exposure of the task set over a specific discrete duration of the EDF-scheduled workload. This function is then integrated into existing techniques for deterministic timing analysis, using processor demand bound techniques, to produce a new tractable analysis method which analyzes a specific, easily calculable duration of the worst-case workload to check for overload following the critical instant under errors. The method allows to carry out a stochastic safety analysis which is suitable to be ingrained as part of a safetycase for SIL and ASIL demonstration in critical avionic and automotive system. The method is distinct from previous work, specifically breaking assumption of error periodicity as considered in [14], and providing new, more accurate expressions for error quantification and timing analysis for EDF than those considered in [15].

div.head: D. Structure
div.p: The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section II develops the mathematical framework, including the task/scheduling and error models. Scheduling and timing analysis is treated in Section III, along with a worked example to illustrate key concepts. Section IV presents conclusions and outlines areas for future work.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: The single processor (or broadcast network) system can be represented by a set T of n recurring (periodic/sporadic) tasks, denoted as T = {1, 2, … , n}. Each task is parameterized as follows:
div.formula: 𝜏 𝑖 = (𝑝 𝑖 , 𝑐 𝑖 , 𝑏 𝑖 )(1)
div.p: In the above model, pi represents the task period (minimum inter-arrival time), ci is the (worst-case) computation requirement and bi is the (worst-case) length of critical (nonpreemptable) code section. For simplicity the common assumption is made that the task relative deadlines di are implicit, i.e. di = pi i. This simplifying assumption will be dropped in the sequel, but at this stage allows the analysis to proceed without undue complicating factors. Each task instance is called a job, and when a job of task i becomes ready at time t, its absolute deadline is set at time t + di. If the scheduling algorithm cannot allocate ci units of CPU time to process the job in the interval [t, t + di) then a deadline miss will occur.

With the EDF scheduling policy, the ready job with the nearest (absolute) temporal deadline is always selected to be run, and ties between ready jobs with a common deadline are broken arbitrarily but consistently, e.g. by prioritization through lowest task index. Preemption is allowed to occur if a job with an earlier deadline than the currently executing job becomes ready, however in this situation an executing job from task i can block another job for a maximum of bi time units if it is executing a critical section of code (e.g. accessing a peripheral). In a fully non-preemptive EDF scheduling policy, bi = ci for all tasks. The utilization of an individual task is given by ui = ci/pi, and the total utilization of the task set U = ui. A task set is schedulable if and only if every valid job sequence that could be generated at run-time meets all deadlines [11]. To facilitate schedulability analysis, two further functions related to the task set parameters will be defined:
div.formula: ℎ(𝑡) = ∑ ⌊ 𝑡 𝑝 𝑖 ⌋ 𝑛 𝑖=1 ⋅ 𝑐 𝑖(2)
div.p: The quantity h(t) represents the worst-case cumulative execution requirement of jobs with both release time and deadline in the interval [0, t). The quantity b(t) represents the worst-case blocking that a job may experience in the interval [0, t) due to a non-preemptible section of code in a lower priority task. See, for example, references [1][11-12] for details of the derivations of these functions.

div.head: B. Fault-Tolerant EDF
div.p: In the context of fault-tolerant EDF, a job error can be defined as an incorrect state arising during the execution of a job due to, e.g. electromagnetic inference or other disturbances. A job fault is the inability of a job to function in a correct manner (due to the manifestation of a job error); and a job failure is a loss of service where the required computational results for a job instance are not correctly delivered on-time due to faults. A system failure occurs if one or more job failures lead to the omission of a critical or safety-related service at the application layer. A basic fault-tolerant EDF scheduler design is assumed, in that it will attempt to re-execute a faulted job (if detected) before its deadline has elapsed. One or more job faults will only lead to a job failure if the scheduler cannot allocate enough time units of execution to run the final job attempt to completion before its deadline. In the analysis that follows, the following assumptions are made regarding the nature of errors, job faults and failures and the resulting behavior of the scheduler: (i) the arrival/occurrence of an error during the execution of a job will cause a job fault; (ii) faults are detectable at or before the end of a job's execution (the job will generate a run-time exception or subsequently try to exceed its determined worst-case execution time); (iii) a period of lost computation time equal to a worst-case of cf time units is experienced after every job fault (e.g. the time taken to execute a fault handler or recovery mechanism) and (iv) if the deadline of a faulted job has not elapsed, it is immediately re-queued for execution using its original deadline.

div.head: C. Error/Job Fault Model
div.p: Any transient upset due to EMI or alpha particle strikes affecting the CPU (and its constituent components, RAM/ROM or peripheral devices) can potentially lead to control-flow or data errors occurring. Previous estimates of bit corruption probability in an IC arrange from  10 -9 to 10 -7 bit errors per hour, varying upon altitude [19]. As discussed in other application domains (e.g. automotive systems), error rates may be as low as 10 -3 . The arrival/manifestation of errors leading to job faults and failures is therefore considered random in nature, in the sense that the probability a job faults manifests during a given time unit follows a random (Binomial) distribution with occurrence probability 1/pf . In other words, suppose that the last job failure affecting the system occurred at time t1, then (on average) the temporal separation to the next job fault is t2 = t1 + pf . However, the temporal separation may be significantly less, and oftentimes more in practice. In the absence of any empirical data or specific knowledge regarding the average error separation pf, one may take empirical measurements or look to practical industrial guidelines. For industrial measurement and process control systems, Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) testing according to IEC 61000-4-4 requires a system to be able to tolerate bursts of interference (of duration  15 ms) with a repetition period of 300 ms. As such, a fault model which sets pf = 300 ms and cf = 15 ms (plus fault recovery mechanism activation time) would seem a sufficient choice for many types of industrial embedded control systems.

To model the effects of errors and job faults in the schedulability analysis, the worst-case processor loading due to regular workload generated by the periodic/sporadic tasks (defined by Equations ( 1)) and the effect of blocking (defined by Equation ( 2)), requires to be augmented with workload due to errors and job faults. As such the worst-case workload due to the latter with respect to EDF scheduling with the system model as presented is required to be categorized. Intuitively it may seem that the worst-case fault manifestation is when the first error in a sequence is aligned at t = 0, as discussed in [14] this is not necessarily the case (in terms of deadline analysis) when blocking is present. To illustrate this point, consider an example in which two non-preemptable implicit-deadline tasks 1 = {11, 3} and 2 = {5, 2} with pf = 20 and cf = 0. In the absence of errors and job faults the tasks are schedulable under EDF, as the worst-case blocking that 1 can induce upon 2 is (3-1) = 2, leaving enough slack for 2 to meets its deadline. However, consider the situation in which an error occurs at t = 0, leading the first job of1 to fault (indicated as shown in Figure 1 (top)). Upon detection at t = 2, the faulted job from 1 is scheduled for re-execution, but this execution is deferred by the EDF policy as 2 has become active and now has an earlier deadline; the job of 2 is executed and completes on time, followed by the reexecution of the faulted job from 1 which also completes on time. Supposing instead that the error occurrence is in the range 2 ≤ t ≤ 4, it is the job of 2 which will fault at t = 4 as indicated in Figure 1 (bottom). At this point although a scheduling decision can be made to re-execute this job, not enough slack remains to do so before its deadline leading to a task failure at t = 5.
Figure 1: Illustration that an error during blocking situations does not necessarily induce the worst-case behavior when analyzing EDF schedulability.

Observation 1: The worst-case arrival of an error leading to a job fault under EDF policy must be considered delayed until at least t = b(d) when considering any deadline at t = d, if blocking is present. This is because any faulted job with deadline > d will not be eligible for re-execution under the EDF scheduling policy until all jobs with deadlines at or before d have been first completed.  Observation 2: Considering any job with a deadline at t = d and an error occurrence in the interval [b(d), d), then under EDF policy the worst-case behavior is induced when the eligible job with the largest execution time is affected due to the error. Hence with the EDF scheduling policy, those jobs which are eligible for execution in the interval [b(d), d) are those which are generated by tasks such that di  d. 

The extension of the above to cases in which multiple job failures may occur in an interval under analysis is not a trivial matter, as there are situations in which multiple eligible job failures for jobs having short execution times may not necessarily be as large a workload as the manifestation of a single eligible job failure with a comparatively much longer execution requirement. There are also situations in which the absence of blocking due to non-preemption will lead to worse workload behaviors that that which may occur with blocking present. For example, this situation could arise if more eligible job failures could be packed into the interval [0, d) than in the interval [b(d), d), with b(d) less than the largest execution time of the eligible jobs in [b(d), d). An additional complicating factor is that immediate detection of a job failure may have the effect of inserting a 'preemption point' in the schedule, which could in fact reduce run-time blocking (although the worst-case blocking is clearly not affected). Although the exact categorization of the worst-case behavior could be obtained, this may require consideration of an inordinate number of options and would be very difficult to compute in practice. However, using a recent extremely sharp concentration inequality recently developed by the current author [18], under the assumption of Binomial error arrivals it is possible to to calculate a very accurate upper bound on the worst-case job failure workload, which is presented in the following Lemma.

Lemma 1: Following a synchronous arrival pattern of tasks at t = 0, for confidence probability R > 0.5 under EDF scheduling an upper bound on the cumulative worst-case workload due to failed job executions in an interval [0, t) in an environment with an average error inter-arrival rate of pf is given by the function f(t) defined below:

Proof: As the average fault inter-arrival rate is pf and the assumed arrivals follow a Binomial distribution, the probability of fault occurrence during unit time-step is 1/pf. The R th Quantile of the Binomial variable which results from t such time steps provides a statistical bound on the number of faults for probability R, and modulating this number by the worst-case resulting workload from eligible jobs and the fault handler execution time hence upper-bounds the function f(t). From equation ( 14) in [18], an analytic expression on the R th Binomial quantile can be written as an algebraically manipulable expression of the Probit function. Expressions ( 4)-( 7) follow directly from Corollary 1 in [18]. If blocking due to nonpreemption is present, from observation 1 re-execution of jobs before t does not need to be considered for errors affecting jobs with deadline > t, and since ((t-b(t)) ≥ t) t ≥ 0, the number of Binomial trials performed at time t can be taken to be t regardless of the presence (or absence) of blocking. As it was assumed that an error arrival will cause the executing job to fail, and since any task with a relative deadline at or before t generates jobs which are eligible for execution in the interval [0, t), taking the largest execution time among those tasks satisfying the relationship di  t gives an upper bound on the execution time of the largest valid job executed; hence adding this value to the worst-case execution time of the fault handler cf gives the worst-case computational demand due to any single error arrival. The function f(t) in equation ( 4) multiplies this upper bound on the number of error arrivals (and hence job failures) by an upper bound on the worst-case computational demand of any single job failure; it must therefore upper bound the cumulative computational demand due to failed job executions regardless of the presence or absence of blocking or the actual arrival pattern of any valid set of errors. 

In the proceeding, the number of errors to consider consists of a constant term f3, a term f2 which grows proportional to the square root of the time interval t, and a term f1 which grows linearly in the interval t. The confidence probability R scales the terms f2 and f3 nonlinearly through the Probit () function. The term f1 represents the per-unit average error arrival probability, while the standard deviation in this probability also scales term f2 through the relationship √𝑓 1 (1 -𝑓 1 ). For a given R and pf, all the coefficients in the function f(t) can be pre-calculated offline and stored, prior to schedulability analysis taking place.

If the CPU utilization U' is bounded to be less than some small fixed constant c, the worst-case complexity of evaluating the conditions of Theorem 1 is polynomial with runtime O(n), which follows from Corollary 1 in Short [14]. Since for many real-world applications the CPU utilization can be bounded below the value of some constant close to unity (e.g. c = 0.999), the schedulability test can be made to be very efficient. In practice, standards such as ISO-26262 mandate this utilization constant c to be kept much lower.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: The inherent intractability of probabilistic timing and schedulability analysis of real-time systems in exact cases has been well discussed in the literature. This paper has provided a contribution to the field by considering stochastic timing analysis of fault tolerant real-time EDF task scheduling. New models and analysis techniques for discrete systems experiencing Binomially distributed error patterns have been developed, and an accurate yet tractable analysis has been developed. Further work will concentrate upon extension of the proposed analysis technique to task models with arbitrary deadlines, comparisons with related techniques (e.g., periodic error models [14]), probabilistic analysis of the Constant Bandwidth Server, and extension of the error model to other sub-exponential distributions.
